plan.topic: Tirzepatide not working as well for you as for others? Why weight-loss responses differ: the SURMOUNT-1 spread, lower average loss with type 2 diabetes, and the Nature GLP1R-variant finding
plan.angle: Tirzepatide working less for you than for others? Responses really do differ. Use SURMOUNT-1's spread around the average, with the placebo arm and full population (adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes, 72 weeks), and SURMOUNT-2's lower average loss in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes, labelled as a separate trial. For the new fact, use the Nature (8 Apr 2026) genetic study of about 28,000 people with self-reported data: a common GLP1R gene variant was linked to slightly more weight loss on both semaglutide and tirzepatide, about 0.76 kg per copy. Frame it as association research that may help explain part of the variation, with no clinical test available and no implication of drug choice. Drop the rare-variant semaglutide-vs-tirzepatide finding, or if kept, cite it correctly as Nature Metabolism, state that tirzepatide response was near-normal in carriers, and never imply switching. Close with 'averages, not predictions' and a question for your prescriber about your own progress, then the don't-switch/stop line, the Exp F line, 'Not personal advice', the prescriber line and the closing line.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide Not Working? Why Results Differ #shorts
plan.why: The Nature paper (13 Nov) adds a fresh tirzepatide-first hook to a high-volume evergreen search. Competition is low, and creators have barely covered it. | fact-check: Source error in the brief. The rare-variant finding ('Rare GLP1R variants attenuate weight loss with semaglutide but not tirzepatide') is in Nature Metabolism (nature.com/articles/s42255-026-01656-z), not 'Nature, Nov 2026'. Search reports put it at about 13,725 treated adults, damaging variants in about 0.2%, and carriers losing roughly a quarter of the usual weight on semaglutide but near-normal amounts on tirzepatide. Its page sits behind a login, so the date and figures need confirming via PubMed or another accessible source. The separate Nature paper (8 Apr 2026, s41586-026-10330-z, 23andMe Research Institute, 27,885 people, self-reported data) found a common GLP1R variant (rs10305420) linked to about 0.76 kg more weight loss per copy on both semaglutide and tirzepatide, and GIPR variants linked to nausea and vomiting on tirzepatide. The rare-variant result can't explain why tirzepatide works less for someone, because tirzepatide response was near-normal in carriers. Using it in a 'tirzepatide not working?' Short implicitly promotes switching drugs and confuses the scope. SURMOUNT-1 and SURMOUNT-2 figures are fine if both arms, populations and the 72-week timeframe are given, and the trials stay labelled as separate.

package.title: Tirzepatide: Losing Less Than Others? #shorts
package.description:
Why tirzepatide weight-loss results differ: in SURMOUNT-1 (72 weeks, adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes), nearly 1 in 10 on the top dose lost under 5% of body weight (placebo: about 2 in 3). A Nature study of self-reported data linked a GLP-1 receptor gene variant to slightly more weight loss on GLP-1 medicines; experts say it's not ready for routine testing.
Sources: SURMOUNT-1, NEJM 2022 (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35658024); Nature, 8 Apr 2026 (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41951734)
#Tirzepatide #GLP1
Don't switch or stop on your own.
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
I checked the claims against the sources and they hold up. I found no safety problems and only minor wording fixes, so this passes.

SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM 2022, PMID 35658024): the trial population and 72-week length are described correctly. The share who lost at least 5% of body weight was 85%, 89% and 91% across the three tirzepatide doses, against 35% on placebo. So about 9% on the top dose lost under 5% ("nearly one in ten" is right) and 65% on placebo did ("about two in three" is right). These figures use the trial's main analysis, which also counts people who stopped treatment early, so the wording is accurate and doesn't overstate the drug.

Nature study (8 Apr 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10330-z, 23andMe): it used self-reported data from 27,885 people on semaglutide or tirzepatide. It found a GLP1R variant (rs10305420) linked to slightly more weight loss, about 0.76 kg per copy. The script describes it accurately as "linked to", "self-reported", "slightly more" and "GLP-1 medicines". The Science Media Centre España page (8 Apr 2026) carries expert comments saying the results don't justify routine genetic testing, which supports "not ready for routine testing".

Safety: the prescriber line and the don't-switch-or-stop line are both present, and nothing suggests changing the dose. The title is backed up by the content.

Minor issues:
- The word "averages" doesn't match what the stat shows.
- The script is 121 words, one over the 120-word limit if this Short is in the tight length arm.
- The Nature PubMed record (PMID 41951734) couldn't be opened: PubMed showed a cookie page and the Nature page redirected to a login. The study itself is confirmed through the EurekAlert release.

issues.problem: The number in s3 is a share of people (nearly 1 in 10 lost under 5%), not an average, so calling it an "average" is slightly wrong.
issues.fix: Narration: "Trial results, not predictions. Ask your prescriber about your progress." On-screen text: "TRIAL RESULTS, NOT PREDICTIONS"

issues.claim: The script is 121 spoken words (counting "seventy-two" and "SURMOUNT-1" as one word each).
issues.problem: That is 1 word over the tight arm's 90–120 if this Short is assigned to it. It's fine if the Short is in the standard arm (135–160).
issues.fix: If this Short is in the tight arm, change s1 to: "On tirzepatide, losing less than others? Responses vary." (cuts "Frustrating." and brings the total to 120).

issues.problem: The PubMed page showed only a cookie screen, so I couldn't confirm that PMID 41951734 matches the title. The study itself is confirmed: Nature, 8 Apr 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10330-z.
issues.fix: Before publishing, check that PMID 41951734 opens the record "Genetic predictors of GLP1 receptor agonist weight loss and side effects" (Nature 2026). If it doesn't, replace it with the correct PubMed record for DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10330-z. Give the source date as "published 8 Apr 2026".
